items.title: Why is Nvidia so powerful in the AI world, and what could Jensen Huang’s scandal really cost?
items.summary:
The AI sector is notorious for the amount of circular financing going on – where companies invest in their own suppliers or customers. Nvidia is a key player in this loop.

Investors are already fretting over whether the enormous amounts of money sunk into AI can ever return profits.

While leading AI model builders Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward public listings or fresh funding rounds, both face harsh reality checks. [...] The now multi-trillion-dollar company got its start making chips called graphic processing units (GPUs), used largely for video games. However, these chips – and their successors – turned out to be ideal for the kind of number-crunching needed for training and using AI models.

Other companies such as Google and AMD have tried to make chips that can compete with Nvidia for speed and efficiency, however neither has been able to displace Nvidia from its dominance of the AI market. [...] Computer chips – specifically the chips used to produce and run artificial intelligence (AI) systems – have become a key front in the United States’ rivalry with China for geopolitical power and influence. The most powerful chips are needed for the most advanced AI, and the US has tried to maintain its edge over China by restricting access to those chips.

While the Chinese government rejects claims of espionage, Alice Huang has reportedly been under investigation by the US for years.

items.title: Larry Page figured out something most ambitious people never do:
items.summary:
Larry Page figured out something most ambitious people never do:

"It is often easier to make progress on mega-ambitious dreams. Since no one else is crazy enough to do it, you have little competition."

Think about what this actually means mechanically:

When you pursue a "reasonable" idea, you're competing against hundreds of founders who saw the same opportunity, dozens of VCs who've already built a mental model of what success looks like, and a market that benchmarks you daily.

When you pursue something nobody believes is possible, the competitive field is almost empty. Investors don't know what failure looks like either — which buys you time. And the category doesn't exist yet, so you get to define it.

Google didn't try to build a slightly better search engine. Page and Brin wanted to index all of human knowledge. That audacity wasn't a liability — it was a moat before they had a product.

The same logic applies to SpaceX (reusable rockets were "obviously" impossible), to Stripe (payments were "solved"), to OpenAI circa 2015 (AGI research was considered academic theater).

The most crowded space in startups is the middle: ambitious enough to be interesting, safe enough to feel rational. That's where competition is brutal and differentiation is marginal.

Page's insight is a competitive strategy, not an inspiration poster. If everyone else has filtered out the crazy idea, the field is yours.

items.title: Accurate medical advice from AI can still be dangerous | STAT
items.summary: Some will argue that AI should be a neutral aggregator of information. But AI cannot be neutral: Every accurate answer excludes many additional facts and emphasizes some over others. Because of these choices, AI answers already influence behavior, as shown by the chickenpox party examples. [...] Artificial intelligence is delivering health guidance at an unprecedented scale. Every week, more than 300 million people ask ChatGPT health questions. Now, the federal government is moving AI deeper into medical care to communicate directly and autonomously with patients. Chris Klomp, the nominee for deputy secretary of Health and Human Services, has called AI in patient care the agency’s “holy grail” for improving the nation’s health. [...] Medical ethics pairs the duty to do no harm with beneficence, which is an affirmative obligation to do good. Safety evaluations of AI have focused mainly on the first duty by screening for responses that encourage imminent self-harm, discourage necessary care, or spread false information. Behavioral benchmarking would extend the first duty beyond imminent danger to long-term harms. It could also advance the second duty, which has received far less attention: designing AI to help people by

items.title: Why is Nvidia so powerful in the AI world, and what could Jensen Huang’s scandal really cost?
items.summary:
The AI sector is notorious for the amount of circular financing going on – where companies invest in their own suppliers or customers. Nvidia is a key player in this loop.

Investors are already fretting over whether the enormous amounts of money sunk into AI can ever return profits.

While leading AI model builders Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward public listings or fresh funding rounds, both face harsh reality checks. [...] The now multi-trillion-dollar company got its start making chips called graphic processing units (GPUs), used largely for video games. However, these chips – and their successors – turned out to be ideal for the kind of number-crunching needed for training and using AI models.

Other companies such as Google and AMD have tried to make chips that can compete with Nvidia for speed and efficiency, however neither has been able to displace Nvidia from its dominance of the AI market. [...] Computer chips – specifically the chips used to produce and run artificial intelligence (AI) systems – have become a key front in the United States’ rivalry with China for geopolitical power and influence. The most powerful chips are needed for the most advanced AI, and the US has tried to maintain its edge over China by restricting access to those chips.

While the Chinese government rejects claims of espionage, Alice Huang has reportedly been under investigation by the US for years.

items.title: In 8 days, my AI team finished half as much work as in the whole month before.
items.summary:
In 8 days, my AI team finished half as much work as in the whole month before.

But the gap on the chart didn't close. Here's why I'm fine with that.

Points are our unit of estimated effort. The purple line (Completed) climbed from about 300 points on 2 Nov to 450+ now.

The green top line is all the work we've committed to. It goes up every time we add a task or size one, and we did a lot of both while finishing.

That's why I post a burn-up, not a burn-down. A burn-down shows only what's left, so it would hide most of what we finished.

Every week I post where this chart stands. What do you track to see whether your AI team is really delivering?

AI-built. Human-governed. I decide what ships.

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

Checklist (18) — browser embutido do assistente de IA (EMBRACE / Forever Security):

AGORA
1. Atualize Cursor pro build mais recente (patch silencioso ~01/10, Forever)
2. Copilot desktop: confira ≥ 1.1.29 (fix GitHub 13/10)

NÃO FAÇA

SE USAR CODEX / VS CODE HOJE

HIGIENE DE SECRETS

items.title: If I had to land a $200K AI engineer job in 90 days, I would not get a degree.
items.summary:
If I had to land a $200K AI engineer job in 90 days, I would not get a degree.

I would master these 10 GitHub repos.

1. awesome-llm-apps
The production AI playbook. RAG, agents, multimodal apps, all in working code. 106K+ stars.
Repo → https://t.co/50OD473w70…

2. LangChain
The foundational framework. Used in production by Klarna, Replit, Elastic, and most AI startups in 2026.
Repo → https://t.co/e8juC9sbHg…

3. LangGraph
The orchestration layer powering production agents. The skill on every senior AI engineer job description.
Repo → https://t.co/e8juC9sbHg…

4. CrewAI
Multi-agent coordination. The framework most Fortune 500 teams reach for first.
Repo → https://t.co/Ixp7pBR3sD…

5. Ollama
Run any open-source LLM on your own machine. The fastest way to learn how models actually work.
Repo → https://t.co/x4D63YcRCg

6. awesome-mcp-servers
MCP is the standard every major AI lab adopted in 2026. Knowing it puts you ahead of 99% of engineers.
Repo → https://t.co/2sxxKGwmT8…

7. Qdrant
The vector database used for production RAG at scale. Embeddings and semantic search are non-negotiable for AI roles.
Repo → https://t.co/OfhwKdk0zI

8. AI-Agents-for-Beginners
Microsoft's free 12-lesson course on building agents. Real code, real exercises, real prep.
Repo → https://t.co/J2ijcIpCCn…

9. system-design-primer
Production AI is system design. The repo FAANG engineers use to prep for interviews.
Repo → https://t.co/g52zkFf5MB…

10. awesome-claude-code
The playbook for the tool now used inside FAANG, OpenAI, Anthropic, and most YC startups.
Repo → https://t.co/rprwu6qQsp…

Here's the wildest part:

A $200K AI engineer in 2026 isn't paid for a degree.

They are paid for what these 10 repos teach.

The market doesn't care where you learned it. It only cares if you can ship.

90 days. 10 repos. One portfolio that proves you can do the work.

That's it. That's the whole game.

Save this before you forget.

100% free. 100% open source.
